body_markdown:
Like any subculture, car culture is full of signifiers. Sometimes they’re as simple as a bumper sticker. Or they can be subtle, like embracing stealth wealth in a debadged, rare-spec luxury sedan that only the “IYKYK” crowd will recognize.


When it comes to signifying high-end customization, or what car people envision as “exotic,” nothing in the car world does it quite like the shimmering black-and-gray weave of genuine carbon fiber.


It’s what race cars and poster cars are made of, after all, and for good reason. Carbon fiber is famously several times stronger than steel, and it’s far lighter. To put a number on it, the density of carbon fiber is only about 1.6 grams per cubic centimeter, while steel measures nearly 8 grams per cc. It can also be molded into complex shapes. It doesn’t rust. It doesn’t dent. The benefits of such a material also go well beyond the car world, and you can find carbon fiber in rowing shells, high-end bicycles, medical imaging equipment,[poorly conceived submarines](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0308016124002175) , wind turbine blades, and wheelchairs.


But this widespread adoption, and the fact that you can even buy sheets of the stuff on[Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=carbon+fiber+sheets&crid=2Q9J0OSKZDQO9&sprefix=carbon+fiber+sheet%2Caps%2C193&ref=nb_sb_noss_1) or[eBay](https://www.ebay.com/sch/i.html?_nkw=carbon+fiber&_sacat=0&_from=R40&_trksid=p4624852.m570.l1313) , hasn’t made it cheap. It’s still costly to produce as raw fiber, difficult to shape into parts, and tricky or even impossible to repair when it’s been damaged. For the most part, it’s still the stuff of supercars, and it’s still one of the priciest automotive components to produce, work with, and fix. Why is that?


Science Museum Group Collection


The first recorded uses of “carbon fibers” date back to the second half of the nineteenth century, as filaments in incandescent light bulbs. It wasn’t until the 1960s that chemical and manufacturing advancements allowed carbon fiber’s use on a larger scale and in structural applications, and by the end of the decade there were carbon-fiber fans being used in jet engines. In the ‘70s, the AV-8B Harrier II ground-attack aircraft made extensive use of carbon fiber in its construction, and by the early ‘80s commercial airliners started using carbon fiber for structures like flaps and fairings.


A glass tube is labelled *1st sample of carbon fibers made by Courtaulds heat treated at the Royal Aircraft Establishment for 1 hour at 2500 degree C on 15.9.65.*


SSPL/Getty Images


The first production batch of carbon fiber made by Courtaulds Ltd. (a U.K. based manufacturer) circa 1966.


SSPL/Getty Images


Made at the RAE, early pre-preg is the name given to composite fabrics made from fibers that have been pre-impregnated with resin.


SSPL/Getty Images


Advancements in aerospace often trickle down to cars (spoilers, disc brakes, etc.), and the exotic woven material soon found its way to the race track. Specifically, the high-tech gauntlet of Formula 1. Both Lotus and McLaren developed carbon-fiber composite chassis for the 1981 season, and all the major teams were using carbon-fiber tubs by the mid-‘80s. Carbon-fiber components soon found their way to street cars, and in 1990 both the[Jaguar XJR-15](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/jaguar/xjr~15/1990/1990-jaguar-xjr~15-base?id=aCn1I000000DHzJSAW) and the obscure[MCA Centenaire](https://www.hagerty.com/media/market-trends/youd-have-to-be-a-millionaire-to-buy-the-centenaire-the-first-monegasque-supercar/) debuted with full carbon-fiber monocoque frames.


MCA Centenaire


Broad Arrow


Jaguar XJR-15


RM Sotheby's/Rasy Ran


In the 30-plus years since, the material has gotten somewhat more accessible, with carbon-fiber wings, splitters, wheels, roofs and more available from both carmakers and aftermarket suppliers. But it remains a pricey material to buy and a difficult, time-consuming one to work with. The only road cars with full carbon bodies and/or chassis are still high-end exotics.


## It’s Hard to Manufacture


The expense starts right at the very beginning, because carbon fiber is a complex material that takes intense amounts of energy, heavy-duty equipment, and multiple careful processes to produce. Most commercial carbon fiber (90%, according to most sources) starts as a polymer material called polyacrylonitrile (PAN for short). It’s petroleum-based, so its price also varies with oil markets and chemical supply chains.


PAN is referred to as the chemical “precursor” to carbon fiber, and turning it into actual carbon fibers involves several steps. It is first spun into very fine strands, then washed and stretched. The oxidation cycle follows, during which the fiber is heated at moderate temperatures in an oxygen-controlled environment to stabilize the structure at the molecular level.


A single carbon filament running across a human hair.


Then, during carbonization, the temperature rises to 1800 to 2700 degrees Fahrenheit to remove all non-carbon elements, purifying the material. The graphitization step raises the temp again to over 5400 degrees, which further stiffens the material. The fibers can then be bundled together to form something called tows before being woven into sheets. The weave needs precise fiber alignment for structural rigidity, but these sheets are still quite flexible. What really gives a carbon fiber part or structure its stiffness is when it is bonded to an epoxy resin, which allows it to be formed into a rigid shape. This requires curing, which is its own tightly controlled process. Some carbon fiber parts are also cured in a high-pressure (and high-priced) vessel called an autoclave.


Extreme heat and long, uninterrupted production cycles add up to quite the power bill. And emissions. For each kilogram of carbon fiber produced, according to[one manufacturer](https://www.cf-composites.toray/aboutus/sustainability/lci.html) , 20 kg of CO2 are emitted. (Some companies do recycle carbon fiber, including McLaren’s Formula 1 team, but the practice isn’t widespread). Additional cost factors include specialized pieces of equipment and specialized labor. Producing carbon fiber also produces waste and by-products, the disposal of which is regulated. Mistakes in any of the above steps can also compromise an entire batch of carbon fiber, which produces even more waste.


A McLaren F1 technician working with a carbon fiber part prepares it for heating and curing in an autoclave.


Darren Heath/Getty Images


The carbon fiber industry is growing. According to one[report](https://www.compositesworld.com/news/ata-2025-global-carbon-fiber-composites-market-report-documents-record-demand) , global demand reached 224,510 metric tons in 2025, up nearly 44% from 2024, with wind turbine blade production being the dominant driver of that growth. China’s operational capacity also exceeded half of the worldwide total last year for the first time. But a growing supply, and a growing number of suppliers, haven’t necessarily made things cheaper. Japanese firm Toray Industries, currently the world’s largest producer of carbon fiber, announced a price hike of 10 to 20% effective this January.


And, relative to other material industries like steel or aluminum, carbon fiber is still small potatoes. According to the World Steel Association, global demand is expected to reach[1.77B metric tons](https://www.grandviewresearch.com/industry-analysis/steel-market) in 2026. Global aluminum production, meanwhile, measured in at nearly[74M tons](https://www.aluminyumyapi.com/en/news/world-primary-aluminium-production-growth-hits-5-year-low-in-2025_244) at the end of last year. Metals like these can be converted from raw ore into a bulk material at a large scale, and relatively quickly, through processes that have been developed over hundreds of years. Carbon fiber can’t yet be produced so quickly. Consider, too, the speed at which a car factory can stamp out something like a steel body panel, and how that process can’t be repeated with carbon fiber because of all the extra, precise steps involved. Economies of scale keep costs higher, because production is lower.


A worker operates a carbon fiber production line at a Chinese manufacturing plant.


Wang Chun/VCG/Getty Images


## It’s Difficult to Work with


Turning raw carbon fiber into a usable component adds another layer of difficulty or cost. Carbon fiber is often supplied as woven fabric pre-impregnated with resin. These “prepregs” need special storage and handling, while parts are often cured under heat and pressure in autoclaves. Tooling for molds can be[pricey](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=q8g75De09eM) , especially for bespoke or small-scale runs of parts.


Jonathon Garvin owns[HTX Carbon Fiber Composites](https://htxcarbonfiber.com/) , a shop north of Houston. He’s been working with the stuff since 2016, when he installed an aftermarket carbon fiber hood on his Subaru and hit a deer a week later. “I was like, ‘I really don’t want to pay that kind of money again,’ so I figured I’d fix it myself. Five hoods later, I got it all right, and it kind of just went from there.” Today he makes and repairs carbon pieces like hoods, wings, engine covers, gauge pods, motorcycle fairings, etc.


HTX Carbon Fiber Composites


HTX Carbon Fiber Composites


Garvin likens carbon fiber to “fiberglass’ mean twin sister,” and that the two materials are similar when it comes to fabricating and fixing, but that there are more things to worry about with carbon fiber, like consistency of the weave, that make working with it more difficult.


As with working on conventional metal bodywork, much of the cost comes down to prepping and time. “When you spray it with clear coat, that’s just like doing[paint](https://www.hagerty.com/media/market-trends/why-is-paint-so-expensive/) ,” says Garvin. “You have to make sure everything’s smooth, spray it, and then if you have orange peel, you have to sand that. I spend so much of my time sanding, it’s ridiculous.”


Making even a one-piece hood from scratch, according to Garvin, can take several days, from making the mold to all the prep work, curing, and finishing. He also uses two different techniques, wet layup and vacuum infusion, when creating a part. In wet layup, he applies liquid resin to the bare carbon fiber by hand, then places it in the mold. In vacuum infusion, he lays the fabric in the mold dry, then seals it in a special plastic bag and runs a vacuum to draw the resin through it. He prefers the vacuum infusion because “I feel like it gives you a tighter, cleaner part with less waste.” Regardless, working with any of these techniques is time-consuming and requires a knowledgeable, experienced hand.


## It’s Difficult to Repair


Mark Capilitan/Sutton Images


Per unit of weight, carbon fiber has about five times as much tensile strength as steel. But it’s not invincible. It does break, sometimes[spectacularly](https://www.youtube.com/shorts/sv8VVdmsWxg) , and structural damage can easily total a car. While Garvin fabricates pieces, including some one-off components, most of his customers are people who have damaged pieces like splitters and spoilers and need them repaired. This takes prep work, curing, sanding, and finishing just like making a part does.


Sometimes people bring him a part so damaged that it would be more logical to just replace it, but aftermarket carbon-fiber pieces are often made in small batches and are impossible to replace. He points to a banged-up custom splitter from a customer’s M3, noting that “this thing looks like it’s done for, but they don’t make them anymore, and the guy who owns this is sentimental and wants this specific one in this specific shape,” and is willing to pay for the time to get it right.


To contrast again with metal, steel and aluminum readily show damage. They tolerate being worked and can be welded. Carbon fiber, meanwhile, requires a more surgical approach of cutting out damaged material, bonding in new materials, and curing the patch.


Darren Heath/Getty Images


Many high-end performance cars today don’t just have carbon-fiber wings and doodads; they also have full carbon bodies and frames, and things get a little (or a lot) more complicated when proprietary or structural components sustain damage. The carmakers themselves sometimes get involved. In 2011, for example, Lamborghini worked with aircraft company Boeing to create a team of on-demand “[Flying Doctors](https://www.digitaltrends.com/cars/lamborghini-flying-doctors/) ,” who travel around the world to mend damaged carbon fiber on its cars, using X-rays and ultrasound technology to assess damage under the surface, with repairs ranging from a few hours to over a week.


But not everybody has access to a squad of Italian carbon-fiber wizards. “What ‘can be repaired’ in the carbon fiber world vs. what most manufacturers allow are two very different things,” says Chase Richman, Hagerty’s senior manager of Auto Material Damage and Vendor Relations. “Most of the manufacturers that utilize carbon fiber as structural components do not even allow repair, and body/structural carbon components almost always require complete replacement.”


Cheng Xin/Getty Images


Predictably, damage to a structural component that is unrepairable often results in a total loss from an insurance standpoint, though Richman notes that “some super-rare and expensive cars can get an entire replacement body from the factory. Figure a $2M car that needs a $200K body; that’s still repairable.” He also recounts a recent total loss on a car that had some of its body panels melted due to another vehicle on fire nearby, and that the manufacturer was “non-committal as to whether or not the heat in the vicinity could have weakened the carbon monocoque.”


## It Ages


Because it’s a relatively new material, there isn’t a ton of insight out there as to how carbon fiber ages or degrades over time. Most of the oldest vehicles to make heavy use of the material are historic race cars that see little use and a lot of maintenance, or valuable supercars that are similarly treated. Both race cars and supercars spend most of their time inside, but more mainstream vehicles and even daily drivers that have carbon pieces see more sunshine.


While the carbon fiber itself is durable and UV-resistant, the various coatings that surround it are more prone to issues. The most common signs of aging on a carbon-fiber material are a degrading clear coat as well as a yellow and/or cloudy appearance. Over time, UV radiation can break down the chains of polymers within the epoxy, which results not just in yellowing but also general fading and even cracking. This is a known issue with[BMW’s](https://www.theautopian.com/exposed-carbon-fiber-body-panels-are-failing-spectacularly-and-costing-owners-thousands/) optional carbon fiber roofs and mirror caps, but it’s common on older aftermarket pieces, too.


HTX Carbon Fiber Composites


HTX Carbon Fiber Composites


Fixing yellowed and faded carbon fiber, as well as shallow scratches, is fairly straightforward but tedious. The solution is to sand down the damaged epoxy, being careful not to sand too far down and damage the fiber itself, then apply a fresh clear coat and let it cure, which all takes time. Garvin is seeing more of these aged, yellowing pieces come through his shop for repair, and as for preventing UV damage, his advice is simple: “Don’t park in the sun if you can avoid it.” He adds that some clear coat has UV blockers in it, but that “most epoxy degrades this way with UV exposure. It’s just part of the formula.”[Ceramic coating](https://www.rwcarbon.com/blog/?p=13003) can also add a layer of UV protection to what’s underneath, but it’s not a permanent solution and needs to be reapplied every few years.


## Will It Ever Get Cheap?


From making it in the first place to tedious repairs, strict limits on what can be fixed, dedicated facilities, specialized labor, sophisticated equipment, and generally low production volume, this is an expensive material no matter how you interact with it. Neither Richman nor Garvin have observed anything involving carbon fiber getting noticeably cheaper. Parts and consumables are actually getting more expensive, not to mention added cost from applicable tariffs.


Silas Stein/Getty Images


There are some potential developments that could bring costs down. In addition to the recycled carbon fiber referenced above, manufacturers have experimented with[alternative precursor materials](https://webarchive.library.unt.edu/web/20130213211800/http:/cta.ornl.gov/cta/One_Pagers/Low_Cost_Carbon_Fiber.pdf) like textile-grade PAN or a biofuel byproduct called lignin, as well as faster and less energy-intensive production steps like plasma oxidation, microwave-assisted plasma carbonization, and techniques that lower curing time.


Some of these advances may eventually trim the bill, but major, large-scale changes haven’t spread across the industry, however. By and large, the material used in the automotive sector still requires the kind of time, energy, precision and specialization that add up to high cost. Repair and restoration haven’t gotten any easier or more straightforward, either.


Carbon fiber was an exciting, exotic material when it came onto the car scene in the ’80s and ’90s. It’s a far more common sight now, used on everything from watch cases to wallets. But due to its chemical makeup and what it’s like to work with, it’s far pricier than the more traditional steel, aluminum, and fiberglass pieces we’re used to seeing on cars. It will probably remain exotic and expensive stuff into the foreseeable future.


A car enthusiast removes carbon fiber aftermarket trim on his 1993 Honda Civic to protect the part from hitting the ground before exiting a car show, Washington D.C., August 9, 2026.


Christine Kao/The Washington Post/Getty Images
